anchor: High on a Throne of Royal State
title: High on a Throne of Royal State ... by merit rais'd
short: Satan enthroned in oriental splendour, 'by merit rais'd' to a 'bad eminence': a parody of the Son's exaltation and a model for later mock-epic.
body: The book opens with a tableau of kingship. The Dartmouth edition compares Spenser's throne of Lucifera, the figure of Pride (Faerie Queene 1.4.8), and Verity notes that Pope modelled the mock-heroic opening of Dunciad Book II on this passage. Satan is 'by merit rais'd To that bad eminence': the phrase is an oxymoron, and the merit, as Cowper glossed it (quoted by Verity), is his having dared most against God. The scene deliberately anticipates the exaltation of the Son, who in Book III is declared 'By Merit more then Birthright Son of God' (3.309). Verity suggests that the debate that follows may reflect Milton's experience of the Council of State, which he served as Latin Secretary. The 'consent' Satan claims (2.24) has not in fact been asked.

title: Ormus and Ind; barbaric Pearl and Gold
short: Hormuz, the great jewel-market of the Persian Gulf, and India: the proverbial wealth of the East, showered on oriental kings at their coronation.
body: Ormus (Hormuz) was an island town at the mouth of the Persian Gulf, famous in Milton's day as a mart for pearls and jewels; Verity quotes a traveller's saying that if the world were a ring, Ormus would be its gem. 'Ind' is India. The 'gorgeous East with richest hand Showrs on her Kings Barbaric Pearl and Gold' alludes, as Warburton noted (cited by Verity), to an eastern coronation custom of powdering kings with gold dust and seed-pearl. 'Barbaric' carries its Greek sense of 'foreign' (Dartmouth) and recalls Virgil's barbaricum aurum (Aeneid 2.504). The orientalism is pointed: Milton consistently associates Satan with eastern despotism (he is the 'great Sultan' of 1.348), the opposite of the republican liberty Milton had defended.

title: Moloch's speech: open war
short: The fiercest devil argues for immediate open war: since nothing can be worse than Hell, even annihilation would be gain, and revenge is victory enough.
body: Moloch, already introduced in the catalogue (1.392), speaks first because he is 'the strongest and the fiercest Spirit'. Newton (cited by Verity) heard in 'Scepter'd King' Homer's formula for a sceptre-bearing king (Iliad 1.279). His argument is the soldier's: the fall was unnatural, so 'Th' ascent is easie' (2.81). The Dartmouth edition points out that this inverts the Sibyl's warning to Aeneas that the descent to Hades is easy but the return hard (Aeneid 6.126-29), which Satan will apply correctly at 2.432-33: 'long is the way And hard'. Moloch's logic that annihilation is better than misery, and that 'if not Victory is yet Revenge', is reckless rather than reasoned. The four speeches of the council form a carefully balanced debate, each speaker's policy matching his character.

title: Belial's speech: 'the worse appear The better reason'
greek: Greek ton hêttô logon kreittô poiein
short: Belial, graceful and hollow, counsels 'ignoble ease': sophistry that recalls the charge brought against Socrates of making the worse case seem the better.
body: Belial is beautiful and eloquent but 'all was false and hollow'. Verity notes that tradition (for example Reginald Scot's Discoverie of Witchcraft, 1584) gave him both beauty and fair speech. The phrase 'could make the worse appear The better reason' translates the Greek accusation against the Sophists, brought against Socrates in Plato's Apology (18b) and satirised in Aristophanes' Clouds; Milton himself used it of Socrates in Tetrachordon. Belial's case is that they should do nothing to provoke God further: perhaps their pains will lessen in time. His famous lines on not wishing to lose 'this intellectual being, Those thoughts that wander through Eternity' (2.146-48) are genuinely moving, which is part of the danger. The narrator's verdict is that he 'Counsel'd ignoble ease, and peaceful sloath, Not peace' (2.227-28).

title: Mammon's speech: 'Hard liberty'
short: Mammon rejects both war and submission and proposes building a rival empire in Hell, preferring 'Hard liberty before the easie yoke Of servile Pomp'.
body: Verity describes the speech as a reply to Moloch and an extension of Belial: stay in Hell, but build a realm there to compensate for Heaven. Mammon refuses to return to servile worship, imagining Heaven's hymns as 'Forc't Halleluiah's'. His preference of 'Hard liberty before the easie yoke Of servile Pomp' (2.255-57) uses Milton's own republican language; Verity traces it to a speech in Sallust, where the Roman Lepidus prefers dangerous liberty to quiet servitude, and the Dartmouth edition cites Hughes for the same source. The irony is sharp: the poem puts a cherished principle of Milton's politics in a devil's mouth, where it becomes a refusal of the one service that is perfect freedom. Abdiel will answer this confusion of liberty and rebellion in 6.174-81.

title: Beelzebub with Atlantean shoulders: the plan against Man
short: Beelzebub rises like Atlas bearing the heavens and proposes, as if his own, Satan's plan: to attack God's new creature, Man.
body: Beelzebub stands 'With Atlantean shoulders fit to bear The weight of mightiest Monarchies', likened to the Titan Atlas, condemned to hold up the sky; Verity explains the myth and the Dartmouth edition cites Pausanias (5.11.5). His speech, Verity observes, sweeps aside the others: war is hopeless, peace impossible, but revenge may be taken more subtly by seducing or destroying the 'new Race call'd Man'. The narrator adds that this 'devilish Counsel' was 'first devis'd By Satan, and in part propos'd' (2.379-81, recalling 1.650-56), so the debate was stage-managed: the Dartmouth note compares it to manufactured consent. The vote is unanimous, and the plan's cruelty is underlined by the phrase 'to confound the race Of mankind in one root' (2.382-83).

title: God's decree 'by an Oath, That shook Heav'ns whol circumference'
short: God's oath to create Man combines the biblical God who swears by himself with Homer's Zeus, whose nod shakes Olympus.
body: Beelzebub reports 'an ancient Prophesie or report in Heaven' (Book I, Argument) that God would create a new race 'favour'd more Of him who rules above'. The oath has two models, as the Dartmouth edition notes. In Scripture God swears by himself 'because he could swear by no greater' (Hebrews 6:13; Genesis 22:16). In Homer, Zeus nods assent to Thetis' request and great Olympus shakes (Iliad 1.528-30). Milton's devils know the decree only by hearsay, which is why Satan must travel to discover whether the new world exists. The jealousy implied, that Man is 'favour'd more', echoes the tradition that the angels' revolt was caused by envy of humanity or of the Son, a motive developed in Book V.

title: the palpable obscure
greek: Latin palpare, 'to touch'; Vulgate tenebrae ... ut palpari queant
short: 'Darkness which may be felt': Milton's adjective-as-noun phrase recalls the Egyptian plague of darkness in Exodus 10:21.
body: Beelzebub asks who will 'tempt with wandring feet The dark unbottom'd infinite Abyss And through the palpable obscure find out His uncouth way'. 'Obscure' is used as a noun, 'obscurity', a Latinate construction Milton favours (compare 'the vast abrupt', 2.409). Verity, following Newton, traces the phrase to the plague of darkness in Egypt, 'darkness which may be felt' (Exodus 10:21), in the Vulgate tenebrae tam densae ut palpari queant, darkness so thick it can be touched; Milton repeats 'palpable darkness' at 12.188. 'Uncouth' means unknown. The passage begins a long sequence in which Chaos is imagined through every sense except sight, preparing for Satan's voyage at the end of the book.

title: Olympian Games or Pythian fields
short: While Satan is away, the devils pass the time like Greek athletes at the Olympic and Pythian games, as in the funeral games of Homer and Virgil.
body: The epic tradition interrupts heroic action with games: the funeral games for Patroclus in Iliad 23 and for Anchises in Aeneid 5. Milton gives the devils their own, with races and chariots that 'shun the Goal' (the turning post, an echo of Horace, Odes 1.1.4-5, which Verity notes). Verity explains that the Olympic games were held at Olympia in Elis and the Pythian at Delphi in honour of Apollo. The Dartmouth edition asks why such contests should be the pastimes of devils; one answer is that Milton is surveying the arts of fallen humanity, games, war, music, philosophy and exploration, and tracing them all to Hell, where they 'entertain The irksom hours'. The episode of the singers and philosophers that follows extends the satire to poetry and theology.

title: Alcides from Oechalia; Lichas; Oeta
short: Devils tearing up hills are compared to Hercules maddened by the poisoned robe, who hurled Lichas into the sea from Mount Oeta.
body: Alcides is Hercules, named after his grandfather Alcaeus. Returning from the sack of Oechalia (misprinted 'Oealia' in the first edition), he put on a robe sent by his wife Deianira, who believed it steeped in a love-charm; it was poisoned with the blood of the Centaur Nessus, and in agony he flung his servant Lichas, who had brought it, into the Euboean sea, before burning himself on a pyre on Mount Oeta. Verity summarises the story from Sophocles' Women of Trachis and notes that Milton follows Ovid (Metamorphoses 9.134-238), who also places the scene on Oeta. The simile is apt for devils tormented by their own pain into destructive rage ('Typhoean rage'), and the hero destroyed by a gift from a woman glances forward to the fall.

anchor: Fixt Fate, free will, foreknowledge absolute
title: Providence, Foreknowledge, Will, and Fate
short: Some devils debate predestination and free will and 'found no end, in wandring mazes lost': the poem's own central theological problem, satirised in Hell.
body: Some of the fallen angels sit apart and argue about providence, foreknowledge, free will and fate, the issues that divided Calvinists and Arminians in Milton's England. The chiastic repetition of the terms in 2.559-60 enacts the circularity of their reasoning, 'in wandring mazes lost'. Verity notes the irony that Milton himself argues these questions at length in his Christian Doctrine and in the poem (3.96-128, 5.524-40), where God insists that foreknowledge does not compel. The devils also debate 'Passion and Apathie': the Stoic ideal of apatheia, freedom from feeling, which Verity shows Milton rejected again in Paradise Regained (4.300-08). Their philosophy is 'Vain wisdom all', yet it can 'charm Pain for a while', a striking concession to the consolations of thought.

title: The four rivers of Hell, and Lethe
greek: Greek Styx (stugein, 'hate'), Acheron (achos, 'grief'), Kôkutos (kôkuein, 'wail'), Phlegethôn (phlegein, 'burn'), Lêthê ('forgetting')
short: Milton's epithets translate the Greek names of the rivers of the underworld: Styx of hate, Acheron of sorrow, Cocytus of wailing, Phlegethon of fire, Lethe of oblivion.
body: Each epithet is a gloss on the Greek name, as Verity shows line by line: Styx from stugein, 'to hate' ('the flood of deadly hate'); Acheron from achos, 'grief' ('Sad Acheron of sorrow'); Cocytus from kôkuein, 'to wail' ('nam'd of lamentation loud'); Phlegethon from phlegein, 'to burn' ('whose waves of torrent fire inflame with rage'); and Lethe, 'forgetting'. Virgil's Styx flows round the underworld nine times (Aeneid 6.439), and Dante used all these rivers in the Inferno, placing Lethe in Purgatory. Milton sets Lethe apart, a 'River of Oblivion' the devils may cross but never drink from: Medusa guards it and the water flees their lips, as from Tantalus (2.611-14). The torment by alternate fire and ice that follows draws, as Verity notes, on Jewish and medieval traditions and on Dante.

title: that Serbonian Bog
short: Lake Serbonis on the Egyptian coast, whose sand-covered marshes were said to have swallowed whole armies.
body: The frozen continent of Hell is compared to Lake Serbonis, between Damietta in the Nile delta and Mount Casius, on the road from Egypt to Palestine. Verity traces the story to Diodorus Siculus (1.30), who says that many travellers ignorant of the place vanished there, and quotes George Sandys' Relation, which explains that wind-blown sand covered the water so that it looked like solid ground, and 'whole armies have bin devoured'. He notes that the historical basis may be the loss of part of a Persian army there. The image of apparently firm ground that swallows those who trust it is morally suggestive, and the phrase 'Serbonian bog' passed into English as a byword for a hopeless entanglement.

title: Medusa; Tantalus; Gorgons and Hydra's, and Chimera's dire
short: Classical monsters of the underworld guard Lethe, and the devils suffer the thirst of Tantalus: Hell as the reality behind pagan fables.
body: Medusa, the Gorgon whose snaky hair turned beholders to stone, guards the ford of Lethe; Verity notes the classical sources and Milton's earlier allusion in Comus (447). The water flies from the devils as it receded from Tantalus, punished in the underworld with endless thirst for betraying the secrets of the gods (Odyssey 11.582-92). The exploring devils then find a 'Universe of death', a landscape of 'Rocks, Caves, Lakes, Fens, Bogs, Dens, and shades of death', a line of monosyllables that halts the reader, peopled with 'Gorgons and Hydra's, and Chimera's dire', creatures Virgil places at the entrance of Hades (Aeneid 6.287-89). The narrator calls these things 'worse Then Fables yet have feign'd': pagan myth is once again treated as a faint shadow of the Christian Hell.

title: a Fleet ... from Bengala, or the Iles Of Ternate and Tidore
short: Satan, seen far off, is like a merchant fleet of the East India trade, carrying spices round the Cape: a simile of commerce for his voyage.
body: Satan flying toward the gates of Hell appears far off like a fleet that seems to 'hang in the clouds' on the horizon, sailing from Bengal or the Spice Islands of Ternate and Tidore in the Moluccas with 'spicie Drugs', across the 'Ethiopian' (Indian) Ocean round the Cape of Good Hope towards the pole. Verity quotes Tennyson's admiration ('What simile was ever so vast as this?') and Newton's view that Milton imagined a fleet of East Indiamen, and notes the topical importance of the Dutch and English East India trade. Several critics have read the comparison of Satan to a merchant venturer as implicating European colonial commerce in his enterprise; the 'spicie' cargo also anticipates the 'Sabean Odours' of Eden in Book IV.

title: Sin: Vex'd Scylla and the Night-Hag
short: Sin, woman above and serpent below with hell-hounds about her waist, is modelled on Scylla and on Spenser's Error.
body: The figure at the gate 'seem'd Woman to the waste, and fair, But ended foul in many a scaly fould'. Verity calls her 'own sister' to Spenser's Error (Faerie Queene 1.1.14-15), with a common origin in Ovid's Scylla, the nymph whom Circe's poisoned herbs transformed below the waist into barking dogs (Metamorphoses 14.40-74), and who became the rock in the strait between Calabria and Sicily ('Trinacria'). The 'Night-Hag' is probably Hecate, goddess of witchcraft, as in Macbeth; Verity explains the old belief that witches could draw down or eclipse the moon ('the labouring Moon Eclipses at thir charms', Latin labores lunae). The basis of the allegory of Sin and Death is James 1:15: 'when lust hath conceived, it bringeth forth sin: and sin, when it is finished, bringeth forth death'.

title: Death: 'If shape it might be call'd that shape had none'
short: Death is described only through negations and seemings, a shadow wearing 'the likeness of a Kingly Crown', more terrifying for being indefinite.
body: Milton's Death is all paradox: a shape without shape, substance that seems shadow, 'black it stood as Night'. Verity cites Coleridge's admiration for the way this abstract vagueness works on the imagination more powerfully than clear outline, and notes the echo of Homer's 'like dark night' (Odyssey 11.606). The 'dreadful Dart' and the 'likeness of a Kingly Crown' recall the 'king of terrors' of Job 18:14 and the crowned riders of Revelation 6. Verity points to personified Death in Spenser, the morality plays and the woodcut Dance of Death as precedents, while the Dartmouth edition suggests a visual parallel in Bruegel. Sin and Death are the only overt allegorical figures in the poem; Dr Johnson objected to mixing allegory with narrative, and critics still debate the device.

title: like a Comet ... Ophiucus huge
short: Satan facing Death is like a comet flaring across the constellation of the Serpent-bearer, shaking 'Pestilence and Warr' from its hair.
body: Comets were traditionally omens of plague, war and the fall of kings; Verity quotes Batman upon Bartholome (1582) and Shakespeare's 'Comets, importing change of times and states' (1 Henry VI 1.1.2). The 'horrid hair' is the comet's tail: the Greek komêtês means 'long-haired'. The comet burns in Ophiuchus, the Serpent-holder, a large northern constellation, an apt setting for Satan, as Verity and the Dartmouth edition note; the 'Artick Sky' recalls the north as the traditional quarter of Satan (5.689, 755). Verity traces the comparison of an armed warrior to a comet to the Aeneid (10.272-73) and Tasso. The confrontation of two 'black Clouds' over the Caspian that follows is cut short by Sin's intervention, since 'never but once more' would either meet so great a foe, Christ.

anchor: Out of thy head I sprung
title: Sin's birth: 'Out of thy head I sprung'
greek: Greek Athêna, born from the head of Zeus
short: Sin sprang armed from Satan's head as Athena from Zeus's, then bore Death by him: an infernal parody of the divine Father, Son and Spirit.
body: Sin's birth, at the moment Satan first conceived rebellion, parodies the birth of Athena, goddess of wisdom, who sprang fully armed from the head of Zeus (Hesiod, Theogony 924-26); Verity notes the parallel, as does the Dartmouth edition. Satan, seeing in Sin 'thy perfect image', falls in love with his own likeness and fathers Death on her; Death in turn rapes his mother and begets the hell-hounds that gnaw her womb. The incestuous family is a grotesque counterpart to the Son, 'the radiant image' of the Father (3.63), and to the Spirit, and Sin's address to Satan, 'Thou art my Father, thou my Author' (2.864), sets up a mock trinity which the Dartmouth note relates to Milton's own anti-trinitarianism. Allegorically, as in James 1:15, sin is conceived of desire and gives birth to death.

title: Chaos: embryon Atoms; 'The Womb of nature and perhaps her Grave'
greek: Latin semina rerum; omniparens eadem rerum commune sepulcrum (Lucretius 5.259)
short: Chaos is a war of hot, cold, moist and dry 'embryon Atoms': the raw matter from which creation is made and into which it might return.
body: Beyond Hell's gates lies Chaos, 'Without dimension', ruled with 'Ancient Night'. Its contents are atoms, the 'seeds of things' of Lucretius (Verity glosses 'embryon' this way), marshalled under the four qualities of the elements, hot, cold, moist and dry, in endless faction. Verity compares Ovid's account of primal chaos (Metamorphoses 1.5-20). 'The Womb of nature and perhaps her Grave' echoes Lucretius' description of earth as the all-mother and common tomb (5.259), which Verity cites. The 'perhaps' matters theologically: Chaos is not evil in itself but the material God uses in creation (7.210-42), a heterodox view, since orthodoxy held creation to be out of nothing. Whether Milton's Chaos is morally neutral or hostile to God is debated by critics such as Regina Schwartz, whom the Dartmouth edition cites.

title: Orcus and Ades, and the dreaded name Of Demogorgon
short: Mysterious powers in Chaos's court: the Latin and Greek gods of the dead, and Demogorgon, a shadowy primal deity of Renaissance mythography.
body: Orcus and Ades are Latin and Greek names for the god of the underworld (Verity). Demogorgon is a figure of late antique and Renaissance mythography: Verity notes that Lucan (Pharsalia 6.744) was thought to allude to a nameless dreaded deity, that the name was said to occur first in the commentator on Statius called Lactantius Placidus, and that Boccaccio made him the primeval ancestor of the gods in his Genealogy of the Gods. Spenser placed him in 'the bottome of the deepe Abysse' (Faerie Queene 4.2.47), and Shelley later made him the force that overthrows Jupiter in Prometheus Unbound. The name was sometimes explained as a corruption of Plato's demiurgos, the craftsman of the world. Rumour, Chance, Tumult, Confusion and Discord complete the court: personified disorder.

title: Argo through Bosporus; Ulysses and Charybdis
short: Satan's passage through Chaos is harder than the Argonauts' passage through the Clashing Rocks or Odysseus' escape between Scylla and Charybdis.
body: Two classical voyages measure Satan's. Jason's ship Argo passed through the Bosporus into the Black Sea between the Symplegades, rocks that clashed together and crushed ships (Apollonius, Argonautica 2.549-606); Verity explains the name and notes Juvenal's 'concurrentia saxa', the 'justling Rocks'. Odysseus, warned by Circe, steered between the whirlpool Charybdis and the monster Scylla (Odyssey 12.234-59), keeping to the larboard (left) side. The epic voyager here is the villain, and the heroic diction ennobles him, but Milton then shows what follows: after the Fall Sin and Death will build 'a broad and beat'n way' over the same gulf (2.1024-30), so that Satan's lonely exploit becomes a highway to Hell.

title: This pendant world ... hanging in a golden Chain
short: The whole created universe, not just the earth, hangs from Heaven by a golden chain and looks as small as the faintest star beside the moon.
body: At the edge of Chaos Satan sees the Empyrean and, hanging from it by a golden chain, 'This pendant world'. Verity, following Newton, points out that this is the entire universe enclosed in its spherical shell, not the earth, which Satan cannot see until he enters it in Book III; the poem's cosmos is a small globe hung in the infinite dark. The golden chain alludes to Iliad 8.18-27, where Zeus boasts that all the gods pulling on a golden chain could not drag him down, while he could haul up earth and sea; Verity notes that Milton himself, in his Latin prolusion on the music of the spheres, read the chain as a symbol of the order binding the universe. The book ends with Satan hastening 'in a cursed hour', and the next book opens in light.
